newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa faces pilot strike showdown.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa faces pilot strike showdown.

text.p: Lufthansa AG faced the possibility of a strike Wednesday after its pilots gave formal approval for their union to strike if the German airline does not improve its current contract offer.

The DAG union, saying a strike could not be ruled out, said 87 percent of the airline's 3,400 pilots who are union members voted in favour of a strike authorisation and called on Lufthansa to make a new offer.

But the union suffered a blow when flight attendants and ground workers did not participate in sufficient numbers in the six-week balloting, meaning it failed to achieve the quorum needed for them to participate in any strike action.
Lufthansa, which said it saw no current strike threat, called on the DAG to return to talks since it said an "overwhelming majority" of its 58,000 workers were against a strike.
The company also reaffirmed that it would not change its current offer, which was based on a deal struck late last year with the ground workers union after talks with the DAG had broken off.

The 27-month deal won by the OeTV, which represents mainly ground workers, offers a 1.8 percent wage increase in 1998, a one-time payment of one-third of a month's salary and a 500 mark ($300) share of last year's profit in cash or stock.
Pilots and flight attendants protested against the offer, staging token strikes in November and December that disrupted flights and cost the airline about 30 million marks ($18 million).
The DAG has demanded a one-year deal as a top priority amid reluctance by union members to get locked into a multi-year contract.

Lufthansa has launched a 1.5 billion mark ($900 million) cost-cutting programme in response to the growing competition, which includes efforts to reduce high German employee costs as well as general operating expenses.
Flight crews have expressed concern about Lufthansa's plans to hand over some unprofitable routes, such as the Berlin-Frankfurt route, to partner airlines.
The problem is similar to the one that prompted pilots at American Airlines, part of AMR Corp., to strike earlier this month before President Clinton ordered them back to work.
Lufthansa, however, cannot turn to Bonn for help since German law prohibits the government from intervening in a collective-bargaining wage dispute.

Despite the failure of flight attendants and ground workers to give the required 70 percent approval for a strike, a DAG official said a strike by pilots would severely hamper or shut down the carrier since the number of non-union pilots would be insufficient to maintain Lufthansa's worldwide schedule.

In addition, pilot groups at partner airlines of Lufthansa, including United Airlines, South African Airways and Thai Airways, said they would not cross picket lines, casting doubt on whether the pilots would fly aircraft on Lufthansa code-sharing flights.
